title: Carbohydrate during exercise
goal: Explain how carbohydrate during exercise helps (blood glucose in long efforts, the brain in short ones) and pick an intake rate for a session from its duration.

steps.title: Long efforts: keeping blood glucose up
steps.text:
In a classic study, cyclists rode at about 71% of [VO₂max](g:vo2max) until they had to stop. With a placebo drink they lasted about 3 h, and blood glucose had fallen to 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹. Fed carbohydrate, their glucose stayed normal and they rode about 1 h longer [[c:dur-coyle]].

The surprise: muscle glycogen ran down at the same rate either way. [Exogenous carbohydrate](g:exogenous-carbohydrate), the kind you swallow, mainly stands in for the liver. It keeps blood glucose up and spares liver glycogen, so the muscles can keep burning carbohydrate late in the effort; most studies find little sparing of muscle glycogen [[c:dur-liver-spare]].

claims.text: Carbohydrate fed during prolonged cycling kept blood glucose normal and delayed fatigue by about 1 h, without changing the rate of muscle glycogen use.

evidence.quote: When fed carbohydrate, which maintained plasma glucose concentration (4.2-5.2 mM), the subjects exercised for an additional hour before fatiguing (4.02 +/- 0.33 h; P less than 0.01)
The pattern of muscle glycogen utilization, however, was not different during the first 3 h of exercise with the placebo or the carbohydrate feedings.

claims.text: Carbohydrate taken during exercise spares or suppresses liver glycogen breakdown, while most studies find no sparing of muscle glycogen.

evidence.quote: In addition to this, exogenous carbohydrates can spare or even completely suppress liver glycogen breakdown
most of the studies assessing whole muscle glycogen utilization did not see this effect

steps.title: One-hour efforts: the mouth and the brain
steps.text:
In a 1 h race, glycogen doesn't run out, yet carbohydrate still helps. Cyclists who rinsed a 6.4% [maltodextrin](g:maltodextrin) drink around the mouth for 5 s, then spat it out, finished a [time trial](g:time-trial) of about 1 h in 59.6 min, against 61.4 min when rinsing water [[c:dur-rinse-carter]].

Nothing was swallowed, so the effect can't be fuel. Brain scans show that glucose in the mouth activates reward-related brain regions that an artificial sweetener doesn't reach [[c:dur-rinse-brain]]. A [mouth rinse](g:mouth-rinse) seems to act on the brain's drive to keep pushing, not on the muscles.

claims.text: Rinsing (not swallowing) a carbohydrate drink improved 1 h cycling time-trial performance compared with a water rinse.

evidence.quote: Performance time was significantly improved with CHO compared with PLA (59.57 +/- 1.50 min vs 61.37 +/- 1.56 min, respectively, P = 0.011).
Subjects were not allowed to swallow either the CHO solution or water, and each mouthful was spat out after a 5-s rinse.

claims.text: Glucose in the mouth activates reward-related brain regions that do not respond to the sweetener saccharin.

evidence.quote: The corresponding fMRI study (Study 1B) revealed that oral exposure to glucose activated reward-related brain regions, including the anterior cingulate cortex and striatum, which were unresponsive to saccharin.

steps.title: How big is the mouth-rinse effect?
steps.text:
Dozens of trials have tested the rinse since. A 2026 [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 90 crossover trials found a small benefit for performance time, distance and speed, with an [effect size](g:effect-size) of about 0.15–0.17, mainly in men [[c:dur-rinse-meta]].

In practice, for efforts of about 45–75 min, a rinse and small sips of a sports drink help about equally [[c:dur-rinse-practice]]. Swallowing is fine if your gut copes; the rinse is the option when drinking makes you feel sick, as on the aero bars in a hard time trial.

claims.text: Across 90 controlled trials, a carbohydrate mouth rinse gives a small benefit to time, distance and speed performance, shown mainly in men.

evidence.quote: The available evidence suggests that CHO mouth rinse can produce a small, outcome-dependent ergogenic effect in distance covered, performance time and speed performance as well as small improvements in workload, with less robust evidence for MVC-evidence that mainly applies to male participants.

claims.text: In efforts of about 1 h, a carbohydrate mouth rinse and drinking small amounts of carbohydrate give similar benefits.

evidence.quote: In most conditions, the performance effects with the mouth rinse were similar to ingesting the carbohydrate drink, so there does not seem to be a disadvantage of consuming the drink
During sustained high-intensity sports lasting ~1 h, small amounts of carbohydrate, including even mouth-rinsing, enhance performance via central nervous system effects.

steps.title: How much per hour
steps.text:
Guidelines scale intake with how long the effort lasts [[c:dur-guidelines]]:

| Duration | Carbohydrate |
|---|---|
| under ~45 min | none needed |
| ~45–75 min | mouth rinse or small amounts |
| 1–2.5 h | 30–60 g·h⁻¹ |
| over 2.5 h | up to 90 g·h⁻¹ (glucose + fructose) |

The targets are absolute, in grams per hour, not per kg: the limit is how fast the gut absorbs, and that doesn't grow with body size [[c:dur-absolute]]. Go lower when the absolute intensity is low: a 5 h marathoner may burn little more carbohydrate than 90 g·h⁻¹ in total [[c:dur-low-intensity]].

claims.text: Guidelines advise small amounts or a mouth rinse for efforts of about 1 h, 30–60 g·h⁻¹ for longer efforts, and up to 90 g·h⁻¹ beyond about 2.5 h.

evidence.quote: While 30-60 g · h(-1) is an appropriate target for sports of longer duration, events >2.5 h may benefit from higher intakes of up to 90 g · h(-1).
Studies have shown that during exercise lasting approximately 1 h in duration, a mouth rinse or small amounts of carbohydrate can result in a performance benefit.

claims.text: Carbohydrate intake during exercise is advised in absolute amounts, because absorption, the limiting step, does not depend on body weight.

evidence.quote: Carbohydrate intake advice is independent of body weight as well as training status.
The reason for this lack of correlation between BW and exogenous carbohydrate oxidation is probably that the limiting factor is carbohydrate absorption and absorption is largely independent of BW.

claims.text: At low absolute intensity, such as a 5 h marathon, total carbohydrate use is low and intake targets should be adjusted down.

evidence.quote: It is unlikely that the runner who completes the marathon in 5 h would not necessarily need an intake of 90 g of carbohydrate per hour as this would be close to, or could even exceed, the total carbohydrate use at that absolute exercise intensity.

steps.title: More helps, up to a point
steps.text:
In the largest dose study, 51 cyclists and triathletes rode 2 h, then a 20 km time trial, taking 0 to 120 g·h⁻¹ of a glucose, fructose and maltodextrin drink. Performance improved with the dose: about 1% at 9 g·h⁻¹, 3% at 31 g·h⁻¹ and 4.7% at 78 g·h⁻¹, and beyond that the gains flattened [[c:dur-dose-curve]].

So most of the benefit comes from the first 60–80 g·h⁻¹. To plan a session, multiply the rate by the hours: 3 h at 60 g·h⁻¹ is 180 g, which you then split into drinks, gels or food.

claims.text: Performance rises with carbohydrate dose in a curved way, with the best performance around 78 g·h⁻¹ and smaller gains above it.

evidence.quote: We estimate incremental performance improvements of 1.0%, 2.0%, 3.0%, 4.0%, and 4.7% at 9, 19, 31, 48, and 78 g·h, respectively, with diminishing performance enhancement seen at CHO levels >78 g·h(-1).

steps.title: Total carbohydrate for a session
steps.problem: A triathlete rides 2 h 30 min and aims for 60 g·h⁻¹. How much carbohydrate does she need to carry?
steps: Turn the time into hours: 2 h 30 min = 2.5 h (30 min is half an hour, not 0.3 h).
Total = rate × time = 60 g·h⁻¹ × 2.5 h = 150 g.
Check against the guideline: 2.5 h sits at the border, so 60 g·h⁻¹ is sensible; a longer ride could go higher with glucose + fructose.

points: In long efforts, carbohydrate you swallow keeps blood glucose up and spares liver glycogen; it barely slows muscle glycogen use.
In efforts of about 1 h, a carbohydrate mouth rinse helps through the brain, not as fuel; the benefit is small but real.
Guidelines: under ~45 min nothing; ~45–75 min rinse or small amounts; 1–2.5 h 30–60 g·h⁻¹; over 2.5 h up to 90 g·h⁻¹ with glucose + fructose.
Targets are in g·h⁻¹, not per kg, because gut absorption sets the limit; go lower when the absolute intensity is low.
Benefit rises with dose up to about 80 g·h⁻¹, then flattens. Session total = rate × hours.

variants.stem: Carbohydrate fed during a long ride let cyclists go about 1 h longer before they had to stop. What did it mainly do?

options.text: Kept blood glucose up as the liver ran low
options.why: Right: blood glucose stayed normal, and the swallowed carbohydrate stood in for the liver late in the ride.

options.text: Slowed the use of muscle glycogen
options.why: Muscle glycogen ran down at the same rate with and without carbohydrate in that study.

options.text: Made fat the main fuel from the start
options.why: Feeding carbohydrate keeps carbohydrate burning high; it doesn't switch the body to fat.

options.text: Raised VO₂max for the rest of the ride
options.why: VO₂max is a capacity set by the heart and muscles; a drink doesn't raise it.

variants.stem: Three hours into a hard ride with no food, a cyclist's blood glucose is 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ and her [RER](g:rer) is falling. What best explains why she can't hold the pace?

options.text: Carbohydrate supply from the blood is failing as the liver runs low
options.why: Right: low glucose and a falling RER show carbohydrate burning dropping off, as in the placebo trial of the classic study.

options.text: Lactate has built up and is stopping her muscles
options.why: A falling RER at a steady pace points to less carbohydrate being burned, not a lactate build-up.

options.text: Her muscles have run out of fat to burn
options.why: Fat stores are huge, enough for days; the falling RER shows she is burning relatively more fat, not less.

options.text: Her heart has reached its maximum rate
options.why: Nothing here points to the heart; the low glucose is the clue.

variants.stem: A carbohydrate mouth rinse improves a 1 h time trial even though nothing is swallowed. What is the most likely way it works?

options.text: Sensors in the mouth signal reward and drive areas of the brain
options.why: Right: carbohydrate in the mouth activates reward-related brain regions, raising drive rather than supplying fuel.

options.text: Carbohydrate soaks through the mouth lining and fuels the muscles
options.why: A 5 s rinse lets through almost nothing, and glycogen isn't limiting in 1 h anyway.

options.text: Any sweet taste works, sugar or artificial sweetener
options.why: The sweetener saccharin didn't activate the same brain regions or improve performance; the signal seems specific to carbohydrate.

options.text: The liquid in the mouth cools the body
options.why: The placebo rinses were liquid too and didn't help; it's the carbohydrate that matters.

variants.stem: In the first mouth-rinse study, nine cyclists rinsed either a carbohydrate drink or plain water. What is the main weakness of that comparison?

options.text: Riders could taste the difference, so belief may explain part of it
options.why: Right: water isn't a convincing placebo. Later studies used artificially sweetened placebos and still found an effect, which strengthens the finding.

options.text: Nine riders are too few for any difference to show up
options.why: A difference did show up; a small sample limits how precise the estimate is, not whether an effect can be seen.

options.text: A 1 h trial is too short for carbohydrate to matter
options.why: Whether carbohydrate matters in 1 h was the question being tested, not a flaw.

options.text: The riders swallowed the drink as well as rinsing
options.why: They spat each mouthful out after 5 s; that was the point of the design.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis of 90 crossover trials finds that a carbohydrate mouth rinse improves performance time with an effect size of about 0.15. How should a coach read this?

options.text: A real but small benefit, shown mostly in men
options.why: Right: the effect is consistent but small, and the evidence comes mainly from male participants.

options.text: A large benefit that every athlete will feel
options.why: An effect size of 0.15 is small, and an average says little about any one athlete.

options.text: No benefit, because it is below the 0.2 cut-off
options.why: 0.2 is a rough label for 'small', not a line below which effects are zero; here the confidence interval excluded zero.

options.text: Proof that swallowing carbohydrate is pointless in 1 h
options.why: Rinse trials don't test swallowing; studies that compared them found similar benefits.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides a 40 km time trial (about 55 min) and feels sick if she drinks on the aero bars. What fuelling fits best?

options.text: Rinse a sports drink now and then and spit it out
options.why: Right: for about 1 h, a rinse gives most of the benefit without loading the stomach.

options.text: Take 90 g·h⁻¹ of glucose plus fructose
options.why: 90 g·h⁻¹ is for efforts over 2.5 h; in 55 min it's far more than needed and likely to upset her gut.

options.text: Nothing: carbohydrate can't help under 2 h
options.why: It can: about 1 h efforts benefit from small amounts or a rinse, through the brain.

options.text: A big bowl of pasta 30 min before the start
options.why: A large meal so close to the start sits in the stomach; the pre-event meal belongs 1–4 h out.

variants.stem: A cyclist races a 2 h road race. Which carbohydrate intake fits current guidance?

options.why: Right: 1–2.5 h efforts call for 30–60 g·h⁻¹.

options.text: Up to 90 g·h⁻¹ of glucose plus fructose
options.why: That higher target is for efforts beyond about 2.5 h.

options.text: A mouth rinse only
options.why: A rinse suits efforts of about 1 h; at 2 h the body benefits from carbohydrate as fuel.

options.text: None: 2 h is too short to need any
options.why: Even 1 h efforts benefit; at 2 h, 30–60 g·h⁻¹ is advised.

variants.stem: A triathlete's Ironman bike leg will take about 5 h. Which carbohydrate intake fits current guidance?

options.text: Up to 90 g·h⁻¹ of glucose plus fructose
options.why: Right: beyond 2.5 h the target rises to about 90 g·h⁻¹, which needs glucose plus fructose.

options.text: 30–60 g·h⁻¹ of glucose only
options.why: That fits 1–2.5 h efforts; a 5 h leg benefits from more.

options.text: A mouth rinse every 15 min
options.why: A rinse provides no fuel; it suits efforts of about 1 h.

options.text: 1–4 g·kg⁻¹ per hour
options.why: 1–4 g·kg⁻¹ is the pre-event meal, eaten 1–4 h before, not an hourly rate.

variants.stem: A runner races 12 km, which will take about 55 min. Which carbohydrate approach fits current guidance?

options.text: A mouth rinse or small amounts
options.why: Right: for efforts of about 45–75 min, a rinse or small amounts help through the brain.
That fits efforts of 1–2.5 h; under an hour the fuel isn't needed.

options.text: Up to 90 g·h⁻¹
options.why: That is for efforts over 2.5 h; in 55 min it would only risk the gut.

options.text: 1 g·kg⁻¹ taken at the start line
options.why: That's a pre-event amount, not a during-race strategy, and a big dose at the start may sit heavily while running.

variants.stem: Why are carbohydrate targets during exercise given in g·h⁻¹ rather than per kg of body mass?

options.text: Gut absorption sets the limit, and it doesn't scale with body mass
options.why: Right: how much swallowed carbohydrate can be burned depends on absorption, which is largely independent of body weight.

options.text: Heavier athletes burn less carbohydrate per kg
options.why: That isn't the reason; the cap is in the gut, not in the muscles.

options.text: Per-kg targets would be too hard to work out
options.why: Per-kg targets are used for daily intake and the pre-event meal; convenience isn't the reason.

options.text: Body mass changes too much during a race
options.why: Mass changes by a few percent at most; the reason is the absorption limit.

variants.stem: A runner expects to finish a marathon in 5 h 15 min at an easy jog. Why might 90 g·h⁻¹ be more than he needs?

options.text: He burns too little carbohydrate at that pace to use it
options.why: Right: at low absolute intensity, total carbohydrate use per hour may barely exceed 90 g, so targets should come down.

options.text: Slower runners absorb carbohydrate faster
options.why: Absorption isn't faster in slower runners; the point is that they burn less.

options.text: Over 5 h, his liver glycogen refills itself
options.why: The liver can't refill during exercise without carbohydrate coming in.

options.text: Guidelines cap marathons at 30 g·h⁻¹
options.why: No such cap exists; targets depend on duration and absolute intensity.

variants.stem: A cyclist rides 3 h 30 min and aims for 70 g·h⁻¹. How much carbohydrate in total?

options.why: Right: 70 g·h⁻¹ × 3.5 h = 245 g.
That is 70 × 3: the last half hour was left out.
That is 70 × 3.3: 3 h 30 min was read as 3.3 h instead of 3.5 h.
That is 70 ÷ 3.5: divided instead of multiplied.

variants.solution: 3 h 30 min = 3.5 h. Total = 70 g·h⁻¹ × 3.5 h = 245 g.

variants.stem: A runner expects a 2 h 45 min marathon and aims for 60 g·h⁻¹. How much carbohydrate in total?

options.why: That is 60 × 2.45: 2 h 45 min was read as 2.45 h instead of 2.75 h.
That is 60 × 2: only whole hours were counted.
That is 60 ÷ 2.75: divided instead of multiplied.

variants.stem: A triathlete's half-Ironman bike leg takes 2 h 30 min and she aims for 80 g·h⁻¹. How much carbohydrate in total?

options.why: Right: 80 g·h⁻¹ × 2.5 h = 200 g.
That is 80 × 2.3: 2 h 30 min was read as 2.3 h instead of 2.5 h.
That is 80 × 2: the last half hour was left out.
That is 80 ÷ 2.5: divided instead of multiplied.

variants.solution: 2 h 30 min = 2.5 h. Total = 80 g·h⁻¹ × 2.5 h = 200 g.

variants.stem: In a dose study, performance improved about 3% at 31 g·h⁻¹ and 4.7% at 78 g·h⁻¹, then gains flattened. A rider on 40 g·h⁻¹ in 3 h races asks what to change. Best advice?

options.text: Build up to about 80 g·h⁻¹; going far beyond adds little
options.why: Right: the curve still rises between 40 and about 80 g·h⁻¹, then flattens.

options.text: Go straight to 120 g·h⁻¹, since gains rise in a straight line
options.why: The relationship is curved: gains shrink above about 78 g·h⁻¹.

options.text: Change nothing: above 30 g·h⁻¹ nothing improves
options.why: Performance kept improving up to about 78 g·h⁻¹ in the study.

options.text: Drop to 10 g·h⁻¹, since small amounts work best
options.why: Small doses gave the smallest gains (about 1% at 9 g·h⁻¹).
